sources.title: How to Ease Your Child's Separation Anxiety
sources.publisher: American Academy of Pediatrics, HealthyChildren.org (Wendy Sue Swanson, MD, FAAP; updated 5/11/2026)
sources.quote: keep the goodbye short and sweet. If you linger, the transition time does too. So will the anxiety. ... provide specifics that your child understands. If you know you'll be back by 3 p.m., tell it to your child on their terms; for example, say, "I'll be back after nap time and before afternoon snack." ... our children stop crying within minutes of our leave-taking
sources.supports: Short goodbyes; lingering lengthens the transition; tell the child when you return in terms tied to the day; children often stop crying within minutes of the parent leaving.

sources.title: When a Child Shows Separation Anxiety
sources.publisher: Child Mind Institute (Rachel Busman, PsyD; updated 26 Sep 2025)
sources.quote: If a child is sick and misses school for 4 days, it's not uncommon that going back to school is causing her some stress. ... It sounds as if her absence interrupted a healthy adjustment to school
sources.supports: After time away a child who had settled may find going back stressful again; it is not uncommon. (The article is about an illness absence; we apply it to a holiday break as an analogy.)

sources.title: What is separation anxiety in babies & children?
sources.quote: Separation anxiety is a common part of children's development. ... Read books or make up stories with your child about separation fears. ... Leaving without saying goodbye can make things worse.
sources.supports: Separation distress is a common part of development; reading books or making up stories about separation fears is a recommended way to talk about them; sneaking out can make it worse.

sources.title: What to do if your child isn't settling in at child care
sources.quote: some children settle at first and then get upset later, when the novelty of the new environment has worn off. ... most children stop crying shortly after their parents leave ... Let your child know that you or another familiar grown-up will be back for pick-up at a particular time or after an event that your child understands, like sleep or snack time. ... Acknowledge your child's feelings, give your child words to express their feelings, and comfort your child. ... Always say goodbye, even if your child looks busy and happy
sources.supports: Settling can be followed by upset later; most children stop crying shortly after the parent leaves; tie pick-up to an event the child understands; acknowledge and name feelings; always say goodbye.

sources.title: Separation Anxiety
sources.quote: Don't leave without saying goodbye. Sneaking away makes a child worry that you might leave at any time ... Have a routine for leaving the house to go to child care.
sources.supports: Say goodbye instead of sneaking away; keep a predictable goodbye routine.

sources.title: What Comes Next: Back to Child Care Following Shelter-in-Place
sources.quote: you can give your child a kiss on the palm to “hold” all day long. ... Read books about child care.
sources.supports: A kiss on the palm the child can hold all day as a goodbye ritual; reading books about child care. (Written for returning after lockdown; we use the ritual, not the context.)

sources.title: How to Ease Your Child's Separation Anxiety
sources.publisher: American Academy of Pediatrics, HealthyChildren.org (Wendy Sue Swanson, MD, FAAP; updated 5/11/2026)
sources.quote: keep the goodbye short and sweet. If you linger, the transition time does too. So will the anxiety. ... provide specifics that your child understands. If you know you'll be back by 3 p.m., tell it to your child on their terms; for example, say, "I'll be back after nap time and before afternoon snack." ... our children stop crying within minutes of our leave-taking
sources.supports: Short goodbyes; lingering lengthens the transition; tell the child when you return in terms tied to the day; children often stop crying within minutes of the parent leaving.

sources.title: What is separation anxiety in babies & children?
sources.quote: Separation anxiety is a common part of children's development. ... Read books or make up stories with your child about separation fears. ... Leaving without saying goodbye can make things worse.
sources.supports: Separation distress is a common part of development; reading books or making up stories about separation fears is a recommended way to talk about them; sneaking out can make it worse.

sources.title: What to do if your child isn't settling in at child care
sources.quote: some children settle at first and then get upset later, when the novelty of the new environment has worn off. ... most children stop crying shortly after their parents leave ... Let your child know that you or another familiar grown-up will be back for pick-up at a particular time or after an event that your child understands, like sleep or snack time. ... Acknowledge your child's feelings, give your child words to express their feelings, and comfort your child. ... Always say goodbye, even if your child looks busy and happy
sources.supports: Settling can be followed by upset later; most children stop crying shortly after the parent leaves; tie pick-up to an event the child understands; acknowledge and name feelings; always say goodbye.

sources.title: Separation Anxiety
sources.quote: Don't leave without saying goodbye. Sneaking away makes a child worry that you might leave at any time ... Have a routine for leaving the house to go to child care.
sources.supports: Say goodbye instead of sneaking away; keep a predictable goodbye routine.
